title: Introduction and System Architecture
owner: Mohannad Al Ghourayeb | Jad Moharam | Omar Tabsh
paras: The system centralizes incident reporting, threat information, audit records, notifications and response workflows. Its purpose is to help an organization investigate security events, assign responsibility and retain evidence of actions.

Sprint I is organized as nine Flask services using JSON over HTTP and SQLite persistence. Each team member owns three services. The integrated branch now contains nine services, including Mohannad Al Ghourayeb Users and Assets. Vulnerabilities and Asset search are now supplied in Mohannad commit 21ad9fc.

The earlier native Postman evidence uses isolated user and asset fixtures. A newer 33-request HTTP integration run verifies actual password login, real Assets and all three Jad services on one fresh SQLite database. The two evidence runs are identified separately.

title: Incident Management API Documentation
paras: Incidents store the reporter, affected asset, assigned analyst, severity and lifecycle timestamps. Users create their own reports and view their own incidents. Analysts view and update assigned incidents. Administrators assign analysts; administrators and auditors can list all incidents.

Example POST body: {"title":"Suspicious email","description":"Investigate sender","category":"Phishing","severity":"High","asset_id":1}. Assignment: {"analyst_id":2}. Note: {"content":"Headers preserved"}. Status: {"status":"Under Investigation"}.

Lifecycle: Open -> Under Investigation -> Mitigated -> Resolved -> Closed. Skips, reversals and repeats return 400. Existing users/assets are checked. Assignment requires audit availability, then queues the notification. Body values cannot override server identity or timestamps.
rows: title, description, category, severity, asset_id; optional reporter_id
201 complete incident; 400 validation; 403 own reporter rule
200 data array and count; 403 other roles
200 assigned incident; 409 same assignment; 503 audit unavailable

title: Notification and Alert API Documentation
paras: Notifications preserve a user recipient, title, message, type, severity, Unread or Read status and timestamps. Analyst and User access is restricted to the recipient. Admin and authorized services can create notifications. Only Admin can delete.

Create body: {"user_id":3,"title":"Security alert","message":"Review suspicious email","type":"Security Alert","severity":"High"}. Search example: /notifications/search?user_id=3&severity=High&status=Read. Types include Incident Assignment, Security Alert, System Notification, Threat Alert and Vulnerability Alert.

The read operation needs no body and preserves the original read timestamp on repeats. Search filters combine with AND and reject unknown or repeated parameters. An existing user with no notifications receives 200 and an empty array.
rows: user_id, title, message, type, severity; Admin or service key
Admin or recipient Analyst/User; no body
200 filtered array; Analyst own only; 400 bad filter

title: Playbooks and Response API Documentation
paras: Playbooks group ordered response actions. Admin creates and deletes playbooks; Admin, Analyst and Auditor can read them. Admin and Analyst can create and progress actions. Records preserve actor identity and action history after deletion.

Playbook body: {"name":"Phishing response","description":"Investigate","incident_category":"Phishing","severity":"High"}. Action: {"description":"Preserve malicious email","step_number":1,"assigned_user_id":2}. Update: {"status":"In Progress"} then {"status":"Completed"}.

Names are case insensitive and unique. Steps are consecutive positive integers unique within a playbook. Pending -> In Progress -> Completed is enforced. Progress requires an active eligible assignee and completed preceding steps. Completed actions cannot change. Explicit completion time must be timezone aware and not in the future.

title: Threat Intelligence API Documentation
paras: Threat Intelligence maintains IP Address, Domain, File Hash, Malware Signature and Other indicators. Values are validated by type and severity is Low, Medium, High or Critical. The unique type and value pair prevents duplicate indicators.

Create example: {"threat_type":"Domain","threat_value":"sprint-evidence.example","description":"Development evidence indicator","severity":"High","source":"Team local test"}. Update: {"severity":"Critical","description":"Confirmed development indicator"}.

Admin modifies records. Admin, Analyst and Auditor retrieve all or specific records; search follows the per-service requirement and allows Admin and Analyst. Type and value are immutable during updates. Successful changes emit audit events. The HTTP evidence uses port 5104 to isolate it from normal port 5004.
rows: 200 matching list; 400 invalid or empty filters

title: Security Audit Logging API Documentation
paras: Audit Logging stores security activities with actor, action, description, UTC timestamp, severity and originating service. Admin or trusted services create logs. Existing records cannot be updated: HTTP update methods return 405, and a SQLite trigger rejects UPDATE.

Create example: {"user_id":1,"action":"TEAM_EVIDENCE","description":"Common report evidence run","severity":"Information","related_service":"Users"}. Service calls use X-Service-Key. The key is absent from the report and screenshots.

Admin deletion creates a new LOG_DELETED record identifying the deletion. The logical users relationship does not cascade, preserving audit information when accounts change. Evidence port 5105 is separate from normal port 5005.
rows: Admin or service; user_id, action, description, severity, related_service
201 stored record; server assigns ID and timestamp
200 deleted record and deletion audit event

title: Security Reports API Documentation
paras: Reports compute results at request time from other services using HTTP and the caller token. Admin and Auditor can access reports. Each successful report includes generated_at and data_sources. No reports table is created.

The earlier isolated Omar run generated incident, threat and activity reports and captured dependency errors. The newer real team integration also successfully generated summary and asset reports. The latest run also verifies the actual Vulnerabilities service and its report. Historical 503 screenshots retain their original results.

Source unreachable returns 503; a bad or rejected source response returns 502. The isolated report process uses port 5106; source ports 5191, 5192 and 5197 were deliberately unavailable to test dependency error handling.

title: Users Assets and Vulnerabilities Integration
paras: Users and Assets are integrated from Mohannad commit 601de89; follow-up 21ad9fc supplies Asset search and Vulnerabilities. His original route logic is retained; Jad added package imports and an optional shared database URI. The current integration verifies bcrypt password login and actual asset creation. The earlier screenshots still use fixtures and are labeled separately.

The Users service stores profile data, bcrypt password hashes, role and account status. The HTTP integration verifies password login, rejection of an invalid password and rejection of suspended accounts. Access is controlled through signed JWT claims.

Assets retain identification, ownership, type and criticality. Vulnerabilities store CVE, CVSS, severity and the affected asset. The specified vulnerability lifecycle is Open -> Under Investigation -> In Progress -> Resolved -> Closed; the observed implementation behavior is documented below.

All 18 route operations are present. The vulnerability report returns HTTP 200 in the integrated run. The model stores discovery and update dates; discovery source and a separate resolution date are absent from the current schema.

A separate 30-request Flask test-client verification executed all 18 of Mohannad route operations successfully. Requirement probes confirmed that Under Investigation is rejected, Open can jump directly to Closed, and an Analyst can create vulnerabilities. These observed results differ from the specified vulnerability lifecycle and administrator-only creation rule. Full sanitized results are in evidence/mohannad-api-verification.json.

title: Database Design and Relationships
owner: Mohannad Al Ghourayeb | Jad Moharam | Omar Tabsh
paras: One SQLite file is the team persistence convention. Each service creates its own tables. Jad uses read only checks against users and assets for identity, account status and foreign key validation. The integrated launcher initializes the shared schema before starting the services.

Primary keys are integer IDs. Incidents reference users as reporter and analyst and assets as the affected resource. Notes reference incidents and their author. Notifications reference recipients. Playbooks reference creators; ordered response actions reference playbooks and assignees. Action history deliberately retains snapshots after deletion.

Omar owns threats and logs. Threat type plus value is unique. Logs have an UPDATE-blocking trigger and retain a logical user link. Security Reports has no table. Historical screenshot databases use fixture schemas. The new integration database uses Mohannad real SQLAlchemy tables with id primary keys. Jad detects these and creates matching foreign keys; legacy user_id and asset_id fixtures remain supported.

title: Error Handling Validation and Access Control
owner: Mohannad Al Ghourayeb | Jad Moharam | Omar Tabsh
paras: Every protected request verifies a signed, unexpired JWT. Jad additionally verifies the stored active account and current role so token claims cannot preserve revoked permissions. Role and ownership checks happen before protected work. Client-supplied role fields do not grant permission.

Jad body handlers reject malformed JSON, arrays, empty bodies, unexpected fields, invalid enums, invalid integer identifiers and blank or oversized text. Values are bound as SQL parameters. Server timestamps and authenticated actor IDs are assigned by the service. Omar validates typed threat values and query filters and logs unauthorized access.

Mutation responses can report warnings for pending side effects. Assignment is cancelled if the required audit dependency is unavailable; other committed side effects use the outbox. Delivery is at least once, so retries may duplicate a remote event after an ambiguous connection failure.

The native Postman negative cases returned the expected 400, 401, 403, 404 and 409 responses. The screenshots show missing token and insufficient permissions. Newer HTTP integration evidence also verifies successful password login, wrong-password 401 and suspended-account login 403. Password-login results are recorded in the separate HTTP integration log.

title: Integrated System Verification
paras: The updated branch merges the latest main and Mohannad Users and Assets while preserving their authorship. A shared launcher creates the real SQLAlchemy tables before starting the nine services. Jad supports their id primary keys and the earlier fixture key names. His endpoint business logic is retained.

The updated full suite passed 220 tests. The new integration test sends 33 actual HTTP requests using bcrypt password login for all four roles, then exercises Incidents, Notifications, Playbooks and Omar reports. It also checks invalid passwords, suspended accounts, stale roles and database foreign key consistency.

Actual sanitized execution evidence is included in evidence/real-team-integration.json. Passwords and bearer tokens are redacted. The test roles are provisioned locally after registration; no public administrator promotion endpoint was introduced. The result is HTTP integration evidence, not a native Postman capture.

The integration run confirms vulnerability creation and a successful vulnerability report. Scope limits include the vulnerability lifecycle and creation-role discrepancies recorded in the service verification, logical SQLAlchemy relationships, and alert producers that are not connected to Notifications.
